view: Al-ʿaṣr means time, the age or the ages; God swears by it (implied oath by time).
note: Razi adds a report that the Prophet swore by time, but refuses to treat its wording as Qur'an since that would invalidate prayer; Ibn al-Sikkīt cites poetry using al-asr for time. Transmitters: Ibn ʿAbbās (with Zayd b. Aslam, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Kalbī, Abū ʿAlī/al-Jubbāʾī in some sources), al-Farrāʾ. Some add that its changing conditions teach a lesson or point to the Creator, that it holds wonders, or (Alusi) blessings and their opposites; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds variant vowel forms illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays; Tustari's second report is 'afternoon or time itself'; Baydawi/Nasafi/Kashshaf list it among options.

view: Time is sworn by because its changing nights and days, passing days and altering conditions offer a lesson to anyone who reflects.
note: Wahidi attributes this to the people of meanings: day declines as night arrives. Jishumi applies it also to late afternoon (night approaching, day receding).

view: Al-ʿaṣr is the late part of the day, the last hour of the daytime (before sunset).
note: Muqatil adds the sun declining toward sunset; Ibn ʿAṭiyya has Ubayy asking the Prophet, who said God swears by the end of the day; Qatada's version (Abu Hayyan) calls it a sign of divine power like the forenoon; Ibn Ashur defines it as from shadow equal to noon shadow to twice that, through yellowing sunlight, citing al-Ḥārith b. Ḥilliza; Ibn Abi al-Asbaʿ gives 'later part of the day or whole time'.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is an hour or one of the periods of the daytime (unspecified).
note: Qatada and Ibn ʿAbbās.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is the afternoon span from the sun's decline at noon until sunset.
note: Al-Ḥasan and Qatada. Mawardi supports with poetry. Tabrisi: the day's final edge as sun sets and night arrives, complements the oath by forenoon, both revered by adherents of the two religions.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is the evening.
note: Al-Ḥasan, al-Layth (the afternoon prayer is named from this usage), Zayd b. Aslam, Qatada (also rich in signs of divine power like dawn). Zamakhshari/Nasafi: sworn by like the forenoon because both show divine power. Ibn Kathir says the 'time' view is the well-known one. Ibn ʿAṭiyya's Abū ʿAlī: asr means day, ʿasr means evening.

view: Al-ʿaṣr means night and day, or morning and evening; the dual al-ʿaṣrān (two ʿaṣrs, the two cool periods) is used for each pair.
note: Ibn Kaysān (night and day), Ibn al-Sikkīt (morning and evening), Humayd b. Thawr's dual for day and night, al-Zajjāj; poetry cited by Qurtubi, Tabrisi, Samin. Abu Hayyan: either morning or evening without specifying. Alusi: on this view the oath is to one of two unspecified times.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is one end of the day (the afternoon), paired with morning, whose signs point to resurrection and judgment, while the evening signs point to death and destruction.
note: Abū Muslim.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is the afternoon, signalling that markets are closing: whoever has failed to earn must face dependents and creditors, a picture of the approaching Judgment.
note: Al-Ḥasan.

view: The afternoon oath is a counterpart to the previous sura's midmorning: that assures the righteous of rising fortunes, this warns the doomed of decline, with remaining daylight urging repentance.
The oath is by the ʿAṣr (afternoon) prayer, the middle prayer.
note: Muqatil; Qurtubi: the middle prayer because it is the most excellent, an authentic report identifies the middle prayer as Asr (explained under al-Baqara); Kashshaf/Nasafi: virtue shown by Hafsa's codex; Razi cites Hafsa's recension of 2:238 and a reading of 5:106; Alusi: majority identify it as middle prayer; Biqāʿī calls it best of prayers; Study Quran notes 2:238 has other interpretations; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports Zamakhshari seems to prefer it and Razi lists it with an omitted noun, no preference. Mawardi calls it also the best prayer.

view: The Asr prayer is hard to keep because people are absorbed in trade and livelihood late in the day; the Prophet compared missing it to losing one's family and property.
note: Elmalili adds that the afternoon prayer interrupts the period when people are most absorbed in work and trade.

view: Asr closes the day's acts of worship as repentance closes deeds; swearing by it magnifies the prayer and urges its performance, through which loss becomes profit.
Prayer is a human act, yet God swears by it as a noble command He prescribed, not as our deed.
Prophetic report: God will neither look at nor speak to those who lie under oath after Asr.
An unnamed report tells of a woman who confessed adultery, killed her child in a vessel of vinegar and sold it; the Prophet named penalties and linked it to abandoning Asr.
note: Alusi rejects the parallel story of a sinful woman told her gravest sin was missing Asr as unreliable material from an otherwise prominent transmitter.

view: Alusi rejects as unreliable the story about a sinful woman told her gravest sin was missing Asr.
note: Compare Razi's account.

view: Qatada also says the oath is by the time of the Asr prayer, or by the creation of Adam on Friday.
The oath is by the Prophet's era, honored by the renewal of prophethood in it.
note: Study Quran: applied to individuals and history, each generation falls a degree below the previous one.

view: The Prophet's era is the time assigned to him and his community; God swears by it as by his place and lifespan (90:2; 15:72). Their rejection of a call from so honored a setting makes their loss greater.

Hadith parable of workers hired dawn to noon, noon to afternoon, afternoon to sunset, the last group paid double and the others complaining, is used to identify Asr with the Prophet's era and community.
note: Elmalili: the Muhammadic era is the afternoon of human history; some exegetes use it for the era of the best community (3:110).

view: Alusi: some take al-ʿaṣr as the Prophet's era or his lifetime through the Resurrection, whose remaining span is compared in a Bukhari report to the time from Asr to sunset; its honor comes from the Prophet and his community.

Bursevi: the afternoon with its signs of divine power, or the era of Prophethood likened to a day or half-day, excelling as age of the best prophet, community and book; a report says if the community stays upright it has a day, otherwise half a day.
Tabatabai prefers the Prophet's era, given the universal loss that follows except for those who follow truth and persevere, when Islam arose and truth appeared over falsehood.

Elmalili: the definite article first directs hearers to the time closest to them; with the Prophet as first audience this suggests the Prophetic era, the Muhammadic era being the most immediate and comprehensive sense while including the broader meanings.
note: Author and some exegetes.

view: Elmalili describes the era: first phase of the mission amid disorder and ignorance; Qur'an begins with iqra; prophetic light calls to reform; the era has two phases (struggle, then conquest) and the Muhammadic era from Hijra to the end of time fulfills earlier prophetic eras; Qur'anic history divided into pre-Torah, Torah to final Prophet, and final era.

Biqāʿī lists possible meanings: the time Adam was created (Friday afternoon, sound report in Muslim), the middle prayer or its time, the Prophet's era, each person's lifetime, late afternoon, or all time.
The oath is an oath by the Lord of time/age, with an omitted object.
note: Baghawi: comparable oaths in the Qur'an.

view: Al-ʿaṣr is the misfortunes or vicissitudes of time (Ali's reading); the author of Jishumi prefers the first interpretation, time itself.
note: Elmalili: reading interprets asr as dehr, whose recurring calamities warn people; squeezing or confinement may reinforce the loss side.

view: Some narrations identify al-ʿaṣr with the era of the Mahdi, when truth will fully prevail over falsehood.
Tabatabai: late afternoon, whose fading day, approaching night and waning sun point to divine governance.
Tabatabai: time or the age, whose remarkable events indicate divine power.

Exegetes propose afternoon prayer, afternoon time, the age or time generally, Muhammad's era, and the end times; asr can denote absolute or present time, a generation or ruler's era, night, morning, evening, afternoon, afternoon prayer, a religious period.
Al-ʿaṣr covers all its senses (time, late afternoon, day, night, morning, evening) because nothing restricts the oath to one.
note: Tabari: time broadly, evening, night, day. Nahhas: time, late afternoon, and refuge. Wahidi: all valid in Arabic usage. Ibn Ashur: whichever is intended, significance lies in being a period that manifests divine action.

view: Corpus Coranicum: other opening oaths name specific daytimes or night phases, so ʿaṣr probably denotes a particular time, not time in general; if late afternoon it differs from all other early Meccan oaths naming night or stages of morning/forenoon; Cuypers reads it as a general span without justification.
note: Turns on the pattern of other opening oaths.

view: Corpus Coranicum: lexica give competing senses (time or period, time of day, morning, late afternoon, evening; dual = day and night). Robinson: the time when merchants count a day's earnings, linking profit imagery to eschatological loss. Neuwirth: prayer-time meaning remains possible.
Ibn Jarir (Tabari) prefers the age, per Bint al-Shāṭiʾ; Ibn Qayyim and most exegetes also prefer the age; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ follows them.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ confines discussion to arguments for that meaning.

view: Kuranyolu prefers absolute time as best suited to the surah's content and message; the oath calls attention to time's place in human life and as arena where God's acts manifest His existence and power.
Alusi objects that using al-asr for time in general is not linguistically apparent.
Study Quran: read after Surah 102, time generally: vying for increase wastes it, and time's blessing is what people will be questioned about.
Biqāʿī: the oath can encompass all time, in which God created the world and decreed events; its wonders direct people to God.
Time contains astonishing opposites (health/illness, wealth/poverty), resisting a simple account: past and future are absent and the indivisible present cannot be divided.
note: Elmalili adds philosophers' debate on whether time exists (r19). Bint al-Shāṭiʾ adds a report describing time as strangely existent yet like nothing.

view: Philosophers and theologians have debated whether time exists, is imagined, and whether knowledge of it is immediate or abstracted.
A final moment of life can redeem a wasted thousand years through repentance and salvation, so time is among the greatest blessings; time is nobler than space.
note: Razi cites 25:62. Elmalili: life is capital, each unprofitable instant wastes it.

view: Night and day are opportunities to remember and give thanks; the Qur'an connects time and what occupies it to God's dominion.
Time is not to be blamed for misfortune; the oath honors time and puts the fault on the human who wastes it.
note: Arabs blamed misfortune on time (Razi). Muhammad ʿAbduh: Arabs gathered at afternoon to talk, so the oath corrects belief that time is blameworthy when harmful conduct occurs then; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects this (evening may fit better, objectionable talk is possible any time) in BINTSHATI:v2p77/r3.

view: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects Muhammad ʿAbduh's claim that afternoon was the customary gathering time.

Hadith: do not revile time, for God is time/al-dahr; Qashani and Bursevi cite it, Qashani without grading; time is the duration of the world and people wrongly treat it as the agent, God being the true agent manifest through it (45:24).

Asr rather than dahr: swearing by asr honors time and avoids the materialist implication of wa-al-dahr (45:24); Razi: unbelievers were fond of invoking dahr. Asad: dahr is unlimited time without beginning or end, whereas asr is passing time that cannot be recovered. Farahi: asr emphasizes time moving swiftly forward and is commonly used for past time.
note: Asad: asr denotes measurable time made up of successive periods.

view: Bursevi: 'asr gathers signs sworn by elsewhere in the Qur'an, concluding the sequence of oaths about dawn, sun, moon, night, day and duha; God swears by time as a locus of divine signs and self-disclosure. Najmiyya: time's continuity encompasses the Prophet's sainthood, prophethood, mission and caliphate.
note: Ishari/mystical.

view: Ibn Qayyim sees the ordered alternation of night and day, changing light and temperature, as signs of God's power; the oath links human actions in time to their judgment. Ibn Ashur: oath confirms the statement; afternoon reminds of the solar-earth system, day-night cycle, end of daily work, blessings, and approach of death.
Nisaburi: evening is like the world's destruction and morning like resurrection; the world's remaining life is like the span between afternoon and sunset, so hasten a trade without loss.

Mawardi: the time is singled out because it contains the closing acts of the day. Biqāʿī: afternoon is valuable because work ends, rest begins, daily gains are gathered, and remaining hours reveal who used time profitably; it evokes resurrection.
Afternoon evokes humanity's creation late in the world's day, closing period of life and the sorrow of returning without gain; Elmalili links this to al-Takathur.

Time gathers every kind of change, benefit, harm and wonder; the oath draws attention to how people fare in gain or loss within it. Time is the opportunity for action, productive or wasteful; its senses of restraint and bestowal support both loss and the exception.
note: Elmalili r17 (dehr contains every wonder) is in the first of these lists as ELMALILI:103:1-3/r17.

view: Human life is precious capital; Sufis say be the child of the moment; deniers of the afterlife also urge seizing the present for worldly pleasure; people fail to calculate gain against life spent; couplets and poems about days passing and reducing life; time like a ship carrying people to death; elegy portraying life deceiving.

Islahi: the lifespan is a person's real investment and its speed its defining feature; only the present can be shaped; no present obligation can be deferred; time can serve the person or Satan; ʿaṣr means a period of time, with the particle wa meaning time bears witness.

Islahi, with Farahi: asr evokes past events and their swift passage, recalling earlier peoples' exact recompense (virtue brought ascendancy, oppression brought destruction after respite) and urging use of fleeting moments; the merchant who admires melting ice; speed of time offers hope for brief self-discipline for eternal pleasure. Poetic witnesses: Imruʾ al-Qays and ʿUbayd b. al-Abras use ʿaṣr for a past age.
Root ʿ-ṣ-r means squeezing cloth or grapes to extract juice; the term came to mean time (span in which affairs are pressed and turned) or late afternoon.
note: Study Quran: evokes time declining or fading quickly.

view: Related words: the afternoon prayer is named for being deferred from the start of its time; ʿaṣāra is pressed grape juice; muʿṣirāt rain-bearing clouds; iʿṣār a column of dust twisting skyward or a strong wind driving clouds; asaru for a people bringing rain.

Age is called asr because experience and hardship press out a person's essence; late afternoon is asr as the day is brought to a close and the prayer is named from it. Quranic uses: Yusuf 12:36, 12:49, al-Naba 78:14, a whirlwind in 2:266, and the sura itself.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ in Ijaz: dahr is named for extracting man's essence through trial; she rejects Raghib's derivation of time from the residue of what is pressed (BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p416/r2).

view: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects Raghib's derivation of time from the residue of what is pressed.

As noun asr can mean the whole age, day and night, parts of the day, afternoon prayer or time, a group, rain; as verb restraining, taxing, squeezing juice. Variants asr, isr, usr; the dual asran day/night or morning/evening. With the generic article it may include every sense; with the covenant article, one particular time. Turkish usage: time generally, present era, eighty or a hundred years.
Dehr, in Raghib's definition, is the interval from the universe's beginning to its end; zaman can name the whole or any part; dehr also means long duration, remaining lifetime, lifespan.
Bint al-Shāṭiʾ (Ijaz): in this verse ʿaṣr means time (zaman, dahr); a single-form Qurʾānic usage.
The wāw in al-ʿaṣr is an oath particle (as in wa-ḍ-ḍuḥā); the oath's answer is that humanity is surely in loss.
note: Itqan: fifth kind of oath-and-consequent structure.

view: The waw retains its force of magnifying what is sworn by; Tabari did not construct elaborate arguments for asr's greatness. The waw moves from perceptible reality to moral truth.

Bint al-Shāṭiʾ (Ijaz): the waw marks the opening as assertion/testimony to what was denied; it places the human under the pressure of time that squeezes and tests him, extracting his essence and revealing loss or salvation. Exegetes mostly read it as glorifying the sworn-by, which she rejects, noting they ignore qualifiers of the sworn-by object; she asks whether waw adds rhetoric over aqsama.
note: Turns on whether the oath only magnifies or also asserts/tests.

view: All surahs opening with the oath-waw, including al-ʿAsr, are Meccan.
Ibn Abi al-Asbaʿ: surahs open in ten kinds of speech; fifteen open with oaths, al-ʿAsr among them (also in Zarkashi); Zarkashi's list.
Qurtubi: generic definite al-nafs parallels generic human statements qualified by exceptions; verse forbids killing any protected life except for a valid cause.
Ibn Khalawayh: no surah of three verses with ten waws exists except al-ʿAṣr.
A reading attributed to Ali (and Ibn Masʿūd) expands the text: by the vicissitudes of time, humanity remains in loss until the end of time; reported by Ibn Jarir.
note: Thaʿlabī adds that the sound reading is the one followed by the general reciters and standard codices (THALABI:v10p283#3/r16).

view: Thaʿlabī prefers the reading followed by the general reciters and the standard codices.

Salam reads al-ʿaṣri and al-ṣabri with kasra; Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows it only at pause through transferred vowel; Razi attributes it to stopping for breath, not carrying pause into liaison; an Abu ʿAmr report uses an imala-like kasra on the bāʾ.
note: Abu Hayyan: other grammarians describe related pause or movement readings.

view: Hudhali reports the kasra for al-ʿaṣr, al-ṣabr, al-fajr, al-watr from Abu ʿAmr in both pause and connected recitation; Ibn Khalawayh does not limit it to pause.
note: Turns on pause vs connected recitation.

view: Abu al-Fadl: transferring the final rāʾ's vowel to bāʾ before pause is widespread Arabic; poetic witnesses (including a rajaz verse ending fī al-ʿaṣr) and a ḍamma transfer example.

Many readers (Hamza, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Yaʿqub, Warsh) choose a pause or basmala between al-ʿAsr and Wayl li-kull humazah; most make no distinction; the author prefers none, with al-Dani and the verifiers.
note: Turns on whether these four places differ from others.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: The surah is Makkan (Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, the majority).
note: Mujāhid, Qatada and Muqātil, and one narration of Ibn ʿAbbās/Qatada, say Madinan; Tabatabai says it could be either but Meccan is likelier; Alusi: three verses undisputed.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: Order of revelation: after Ash-Sharh/94 and before al-ʿĀdiyāt (al-Duha, Alam Nashrah, al-Asr, al-Adiyat).
note: Bayhaqi: first-revelation hadith has witnesses in Muqatil's tafsir and a sound mursal.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: Ibn Masʿūd mushaf order places al-Asr in the mufassal.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: Ubayy says he recited the surah to the Prophet and asked for its interpretation.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: Before Islam, ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ recited al-ʿAṣr to Musaylima, who answered with a parody; al-Wabr is a small cat-like animal; al-Kharāʾiṭī records the story too.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: Companions would recite Surat al-ʿAṣr to each other whenever they met before parting and exchanging greetings.
note: Qutb adds renewing commitment to its guidance.

topic: occasion, place and order of revelation
view: At Umar's stabbing, Abd al-Rahman led Fajr and recited al-Asr and another short surah.

topic: virtue and sufficiency of the surah
view: Al-Shāfiʿī: if people pondered the surah, or if no other revelation came, it would suffice them; another view says it contains all Qur'anic sciences.

topic: virtue and sufficiency of the surah
view: Report: reciting Sūrat al-ʿAṣr brings patience and companionship with the people of truth on the Resurrection Day.

topic: virtue and sufficiency of the surah
view: Prophet identifies the person in loss with Abu Jahl and believers, righteous deeds, truth and patience with Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali; ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās repeated it from the pulpit.
note: Ibn al-Jawzī in contrast identifies the insan as Abu Lahab (IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p181/r10).

topic: virtue and sufficiency of the surah
view: Ibn al-Jawzī: Abu Lahab is the insan of 103:2.
Follows al-Takāthur: warns against wasting life on rivalry and wealth; Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, Biqāʿī, Islahi all link it.
note: Abu Hayyan: distinguishes believer from unbeliever.

view: Biqāʿī: the surah distinguishes the saved human essence from the doomed and teaches salvation by leaving the transient for the lasting; the name signals extraction; begins with examples of ruined and saved because preventing harm precedes securing benefit; Ghazali's six minerals; clauses map to knowledge, worship, patience; basmala says all perish except God.

The surah condenses the Qur'an's teachings; Qutb: it compresses Islam's way of life and the community's identity into a constitution; one successful path across ages: faith, righteous action, mutual exhortation to truth and patience; Akif's poem; Samarrai: the added exhortation prevents further loss of reward.
Muhammad ibn Kaʿb: all people are in loss; belief alone is not enough, the verse requires good works, counsel in truth and counsel in patience.
Humanity is in loss when people neglect God's rights, follow desires, and do not fear Him.
Loss (khusrān) is diminution, loss of part of the capital; Bursevi: grave because the servant sins against the Lord and immense benefaction; indefinite form may mark a distinctive kind of loss.

Corpus Coranicum: no hymn-like resonance; Neuwirth argues oaths by prayer times preserve the recipient's liturgical experience and give the sura a hymn-like tone, treats the oath as an independent verse; pre-Islamic seer expression; Spitaler's Medina II joins verse 1 to 2.
note: Turns on whether the sura has a liturgical hymn tone.

view: Al-ʿAsr counted as a verse by analogy with al-Fajr and al-Duha for rhyme; a single word can be a verse; verse division is tawqifi (Zamakhshari) or relies on early practice (Ibn al-ʿArabī); some say revelation alone.
note: Last Medinan counter counts Watawasaw bil-haqq (103:3) as a verse and not wal-asr; other counters the reverse.

view: One classification places al-Asr among surahs with both abrogating and abrogated verses; Suyuti doubts it; Ibn al-ʿArabī on rare abrogation of ruling without recitation.

Malik: swearing not to speak for an asr means a year. Shafiʿi: an hour unless another duration intended. Ibn al-ʿArabī prefers Shafiʿi's hour, but for an Arab the plausibly intended meaning is accepted except the shortest.
note: Differ on how large an asr is.

view: Qushayri: whoever hears God's name does not withhold wealth, knows it does not prefer himself, accompanies it does not withhold his spirit.
Qashani: affliction falls first on prophets, then saints, then the best in descending order; affliction is God's whip driving servants toward Him.

Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites Razi's six reasons for the greatness of the age, three for a particular time, six for afternoon prayer, and a case for the Prophetic age; she rejects philosophical and mystical interpretations since the Qur'an explains night and day in accessible terms (28:71-72).
